content: Famotidine injection is a medication that inhibits gastric acid secretion. It is approved by the FDA for use in hospitalized patients with pathological hypersecretory conditions, intractable ulcers, or for short-term treatment of duodenal ulcers, benign gastric ulcers, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It is also used for esophagitis caused by GERD, including erosive or ulcerative forms, and for conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome or multiple endocrine adenomas. Famotidine injection is intended for intravenous use only. It is supplied as a concentrated solution that must be diluted before administration. The recommended adult dose for pathological hypersecretory conditions is 20 mg every 12 hours, with adjustments based on individual patient needs. For patients with severe Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, higher doses, including oral doses up to 160 mg every 6 hours, have been used. For intravenous administration, the solution should be diluted aseptically and injected over at least 2 minutes or infused over 15 to 30 minutes. In patients with moderate or severe renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance <50 mL/min or <10 mL/min), the elimination half-life of famotidine is prolonged, potentially exceeding 20 hours in anuric patients. To avoid drug accumulation and central nervous system (CNS) adverse effects, the dose may need to be reduced by half or the dosing interval extended to 36–48 hours, depending on clinical response. Famotidine injection is also used in pediatric patients. For children under 1 year of age with GERD, the recommended starting dose is 0.5 mg/kg once daily for those under 3 months of age and 0.5 mg/kg twice daily for those aged 3 months to less than 1 year. For pediatric patients aged 1–16 years, the starting dose is 0.25 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, up to a maximum of 40 mg/day. The duration of treatment and dose should be individualized based on clinical response and gastric pH monitoring. Famotidine is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to any of its components or other H2-receptor antagonists. Common adverse reactions include headache, dizziness, constipation, and diarrhea. Rare but serious adverse effects include agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. In pediatric patients under 1 year of age, agitation has been reported and resolved upon discontinuation of the drug. Famotidine is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate studies in pregnant women. Famotidine is excreted in breast milk, and its use in nursing mothers should be carefully considered, weighing the benefits to the mother against potential risks to the infant. Famotidine injection is stable for 7 days at room temperature when diluted with compatible intravenous solutions, such as 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose. However, diluted solutions should be refrigerated and used within 48 hours if not administered immediately. The injection should be stored at 2° to 8°C (36° to 46°F) and protected from light. Famotidine works by competitively inhibiting histamine H2-receptors, reducing both the volume and acidity of gastric secretions. Its effects are dose-dependent, with a duration of action of 10–12 hours for typical doses. It has minimal effects on fasting or postprandial serum gastrin levels and does not affect gastric emptying or pancreatic function. In cases of overdose, symptoms are similar to those seen in normal clinical use. Treatment should be supportive and symptomatic, with monitoring and removal of unabsorbed material from the gastrointestinal tract. Famotidine has a high safety margin, with no serious adverse effects reported at oral doses up to 640 mg/day in patients with pathological hypersecretory conditions.
